content:
Plan for Phase 70 (standing orders) at docs/phases/standing-orders.md, commit bf73a43 on branch phase-70-standing-orders.

Core decisions to review:
1. Two kinds, kept apart. ENFORCED: one order, 'stop' = phase | roadmap. 'Only on questions' is not a third value: escalations, NEED_HUMAN and a blocked roadmap already stop a run under both values. ADVISORY: numbered free-text notes, delivered but never enforced.
2. Storage: project orders in a committed tagteam-orders.json at the root. It is read with safe_read, and a malformed file gives 'no orders' plus a warn, never an exception. The per-run override is an 'orders' key in handoff-state.json, which _derive_top_level_state must preserve (it writes with replace=True).
3. One resolver, orders.effective(), precedence run > run-mode (full-roadmap) > project > default phase. Every surface calls it.
4. Enforcement happens at the impl-approval state write (_derive_top_level_state), not in the watcher. The stop order is applied by rewriting run_mode/roadmap, the fields the watcher already keys on. stop=roadmap on a single-phase run converts it to full-roadmap with a build_queue() queue. stop=phase on a full-roadmap run drops back to single-phase. The watcher itself is unchanged except for one key: the roadmap-complete write drops the run override.
5. Run override lifetime: dropped when the run ends (a stop at impl approval, or roadmap-complete) or on 'orders clear --run'. It survives escalations, pauses and intermediate cycle writes.
6. Delivery: a STANDING ORDERS block in the headless prompt; the same block on stderr for 'cycle rounds' (stdout JSON unchanged); an Orders line in 'tagteam state'; a paragraph in the contract and in workflows.md.
7. CLI 'tagteam orders' (show / stop / add / remove / clear, --run, --json). Writes are refused under TAGTEAM_READ_ONLY; the bare read is allowed.
8. tagteam-orders.json is excluded from the impl scope check.

Open questions I'd like a view on: enforcing at the approval write vs in the watcher; a committed orders file vs one under .tagteam/.

The overall design is sound: keep enforced stop policy separate from advisory notes, use one resolver, and record the transition at approval. A committed root-level orders file is consistent with durable project preferences; no storage-location escalation is needed. Before implementation, please resolve these lifecycle and compatibility gaps in docs/phases/standing-orders.md.

1. Make approval enforcement idempotent under state reconciliation (lines 94-120). _derive_top_level_state is also called by tagteam state sync (tagteam/state.py:856), not only by a new APPROVE. Concrete case: project stop=roadmap, run stop=phase, impl approval stops and clears the run override; state sync on that same approved cycle now resolves the project roadmap order and converts the stopped run back to full-roadmap. Similarly, an override queued for the next run while state is done can be consumed by syncing the previous approved cycle. Specify how a recorded approval decision is distinguished from a fresh approval and preserved on reconciliation, without applying next-run orders to an old cycle. Add regression criteria for both scenarios.

2. Complete the conversion/end-of-run cases (lines 104 and 117-130). Missing/invalid roadmap explicitly stops as single-phase, but the lifetime rules clear orders only for effective stop=phase or watcher roadmap-complete. Thus a run stop=roadmap plus advisory notes survives that ended run and leaks into the next one. Also build_queue raises ValueError when all phases are already terminal, and excludes terminal phases from its queue: an approved phase marked Complete can be absent even though it is present in the roadmap. Define valid exhausted-roadmap completion separately from missing/invalid-roadmap fallback, define the index/queue behavior when the approved phase is already terminal, and specify override cleanup for every terminal outcome. Pin these cases with tests; preserve overrides only for outcomes explicitly treated as resumable pauses.

3. Reconcile the no-orders compatibility promise (lines 153-164 and success criterion 1). effective() returns roadmap from run-mode on an ordinary full-roadmap run with no orders, so the stated block-omission rule would render a new block; the Orders line also changes existing state output. Either suppress these additions when no explicit orders exist, or narrow the byte-identical promise to intentional invariants and state which output changes are expected. Make the full-roadmap/no-orders test agree with that decision.

Reviewed the plan against cycle derivation, state sync, roadmap queue construction, watcher advancement and prompt composition. No tests run for this plan review.

All three r1 findings are addressed in docs/phases/standing-orders.md @ dfc11ef.

1. Reconciliation (sections "Enforcement: decided once…" and "The outcomes…"). The decision is split. add_round DECIDES, only on a fresh impl APPROVE with explicit orders, and records `run_decision` {outcome advance|stop|complete, reason, stop, source, queue/current_index for advance} on the cycle status file. _derive_top_level_state then APPLIES only the recorded decision and never re-resolves. stop/complete re-apply as single-phase, which is idempotent and can never start a phase. On a sync, advance gets only the existing roadmap-preservation rule and never re-creates a queue. A single flag, `fresh_decision=True`, passed only by add_round, is the only way to materialise an advance queue or to drop the run override. So sync, gate, rearm and init never convert a run or consume an override. New criterion 11 pins (a) project roadmap + run phase → approve → sync stays single-phase, twice; (b) an override queued while done survives a sync of the old cycle and isn't applied to it; (c) a sync after the watcher moved on doesn't re-create the queue.

2. Terminal outcomes. There is a full outcome table. An exhausted roadmap (build_queue's all-complete case, or only the approved phase left) gives `complete`. A missing, unparseable or check_graph-invalid roadmap gives `stop` / `roadmap-invalid: …`, with one line on stderr. Both drop the override. The approved phase is always queue[0], even when the roadmap already marks it Complete, so the preservation rule holds and the watcher marks it completed. Nothing can raise out of the approval write; at worst the decision is `stop`. The Lifetime section lists every drop point and the exact resumable pauses that keep the override (escalation, NEED_HUMAN, blocked:/roadmap invalid:/stale queue:). New criterion 12 and a reworded criterion 4 pin each case.

3. No-orders promise. "Explicit orders" is defined as a file with a non-null stop or at least one note, or a run override. Without explicit orders nothing new is written or printed anywhere (no run_decision, no block, no Orders line, no change to the approval write), including an ordinary full-roadmap run whose effective stop comes from its run mode. Criterion 1 now pins byte-identity for single-phase and full-roadmap alike. With explicit orders, the new outputs are listed as intended changes.

Also accepted: your note that a committed root-level orders file is fine; the storage question is closed.

The r1 findings are addressed: decisions are recorded at fresh approval rather than re-resolved by state sync; exhausted and invalid roadmap outcomes have explicit cleanup; and delivery is gated on explicit orders.

One new inconsistency must be resolved before implementation. In the Apply table, every fresh advance writes the recorded queue/current_index with completed: []. In the outcomes table, roadmap + an existing full-roadmap run instead says state unchanged from today. These are different behaviors, and resetting completed is incorrect for an existing run. _try_roadmap_advance reads roadmap.completed and adds only the phase just approved; _select_next_phase then scans the entire queue, using completed to exclude prior approvals and satisfy dependencies even when docs/roadmap.md still has non-terminal statuses. With queue [A, B, C], completed [A], current B, and explicit orders (even just an advisory note), resetting completed on B approval makes A eligible to run again.

Please distinguish preserving an existing full-roadmap context from creating a new queue when converting single-phase. Preserve the existing queue, current_index and completed list for the former; initialise completed only for the latter. Align the recorded decision shape and apply rules with that distinction. Add an end-to-end criterion: with explicit advisory orders, A completed only in the run state, and B being approved, the watcher advances to C with A and B still completed, without restarting A or losing dependency satisfaction.

No other blocking plan findings. No tests run for this plan review.

The r2 finding is fixed in docs/phases/standing-orders.md @ fd4fda3.

"advance" is now two outcomes:
- `continue`: the run is already full-roadmap. Only the outcome is recorded. The run's queue, current_index and completed list are never rewritten, fresh or sync; the existing preservation rule keeps them. So the watcher's _try_roadmap_advance / _select_next_phase see exactly what they see today.
- `convert`: a single-phase run becomes a new roadmap run. Only this outcome records queue/current_index, and only this one starts with completed: [].

Changed to match: the run_decision shape (outcome continue|convert|stop|complete), the Apply table (separate continue and convert rows), the outcomes table (full-roadmap + stop roadmap → continue, roadmap untouched), criterion 11(c) and the `tagteam state` outcome wording.

New criterion 13, your end-to-end case. A real roadmap in tmp_path with A → B → C, C depending on A, and A and B still non-terminal in the doc. The run state has queue [A,B,C], completed [A], current B, plus one advisory note. Approving B records `continue` and leaves the state's roadmap unchanged by the approval write. The unchanged watcher then starts C with completed [A,B]: A is not restarted, and C's dependency is satisfied through the run's completed list.

Approved docs/phases/standing-orders.md at fd4fda3. All prior findings are resolved. The continue outcome preserves the existing queue, index and completed list; only convert creates a new roadmap context. Criterion 13 covers prior approvals and dependency satisfaction using the run's completed list. The earlier safeguards for reconciliation, terminal override cleanup, conversion edge cases and no-orders compatibility remain in place. Scope, approach and success criteria are sufficient to proceed with implementation. No tests run for this plan review.
